strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem: the computational cost of transformer-based visual world models for MPC planning, which is a genuine bottleneck for real-time robotic deployment.
Simple and easy-to-implement method (random patch dropout + randomized grouped attention training) that integrates with existing transformer world models without major architectural changes.
Fairly extensive empirical evaluation across six diverse environments (navigation, deformable object manipulation, precise manipulation) with both performance and wall-clock planning time reported.

Thorough ablation and analysis section: nHSIC information-theoretic analysis, attentive probing, comparison against many sophisticated token selection/merging baselines (LTRP, STAR, Attention-Encoder, ATC, etc.), and noise-robustness experiments for CEM.

The finding that random dropout is competitive with or better than sophisticated learned/attention-based token selection methods is an interesting and somewhat counter-intuitive empirical contribution that could be of practical interest to the community.
Good implementation detail and reproducibility effort in the appendix (dataset details, hyperparameters, training details for baselines).
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is limited: random token dropout during inference and grouped/masked attention training are well-established ideas in the ViT efficiency literature (e.g., PatchDropout, DynamicViT, masked training). The main contribution is largely an application of these known techniques to a specific world-model planning setting rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Performance numbers in Table 1 are noisy and non-monotonic with respect to dropout ratio (e.g., PointMaze peaks at 50% dropout with 100% success, exceeding Full at 98.3%; Rope also improves with dropout), which is not well explained mechanistically beyond hand-wavy claims of 'redundancy' and 'resampling robustness.' This raises concern about evaluation variance/statistical significance, especially given small numbers of evaluation episodes (e.g., 20 for Granular, 30 for Rope).

No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed reporting for the main success rate results in Table 1 and Table 3, despite substantial stochasticity in CEM planning and environment resets; this weakens the reliability of comparative claims (e.g., claiming dropout 'significantly outperforms' Full or CLS).

The wall-clock planning-time improvements, while real, are modest at the dropout levels claimed to preserve performance (~30-50% reduction at 50% dropout, not linear/quadratic as the token count reduction might suggest), somewhat undercutting the 'dramatically improving inference efficiency' framing in the abstract.

All experiments are conducted purely in simulation on relatively simple/synthetic benchmarks; no real robot or real-world visual data validation is provided, which is explicitly acknowledged as a limitation but still substantially limits claims about practical deployment for 'real-time robotics.'

The theoretical/mechanistic explanation for why sparse imagination works (information redundancy, HSIC, probing) is somewhat superficial and correlational; the paper does not provide a rigorous account of why performance sometimes improves with dropout rather than only degrading gracefully, leaving the central phenomenon under-explained.

Comparison baselines (Full-Patch, CLS-Token) are limited to essentially one prior architecture family (DINO-WM), and no comparison is made to other efficient world model or token-reduction-for-control approaches beyond the vision literature baselines that were repurposed.

The paper's contribution list somewhat overstates novelty (e.g., 'novel training and inference method') given how directly it borrows from existing dropout/masking ideas in ViT literature; overall framing could be more calibrated to the scope of the contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and relevant problem: the quadratic computational cost of patch-token-based visual world models during MPC rollouts, which is important for real-time robotics applications.

The experimental protocol is reasonably broad, covering six simulated environments (navigation, rigid and deformable manipulation) and comparing against sensible baselines (Full-Patch and CLS-token world models from DINO-WM).

The comparative study against numerous token selection/merging alternatives (LHS, LTRP, Attention-Encoder, STAR, Attention-WM, ATC) is a useful negative result showing that sophisticated selection does not outperform random dropout, which could save future researchers effort.

Supplementary analyses (nHSIC, attentive probing, UMAP visualization of prediction error, noise-robustness experiments) attempt to explain why sparse imagination works, going beyond a pure performance table.
Reasonably detailed implementation and reproducibility information is provided in the appendix (architectures, hyperparameters, dataset statistics).
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is incremental: it combines a known technique (ViT patch dropout, already studied e.g. PatchDropout) with a straightforward grouped-attention masking scheme applied to an existing world model (DINO-WM). The conceptual novelty beyond 'drop tokens at inference and train with a grouping mask' is limited.

The main results in Table 1 are difficult to trust as evidence of a genuine effect: dropout models frequently *outperform* the Full-Patch baseline by small, inconsistent margins (e.g., Pointmaze 100.0% at 50% drop vs 98.3% full; Wall 95.0% vs 85.0%) with no reported variance, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds, and with small evaluation sizes (20-60 episodes). This makes it impossible to tell whether reported differences are statistically meaningful or noise, undermining the central claim that sparsity 'preserves' or even 'improves' performance.

Absolute success rates are very low in some environments regardless of method (e.g., Block Pushing: Full 22.0%, best dropout 28.0%), suggesting the base world model/planning pipeline itself may be weak or the task setup is not well-tuned, which weakens confidence in the comparative conclusions drawn from that environment.

No real-robot or real-world experiments are included; all results are on simulated benchmarks, which the authors acknowledge as a limitation but which significantly limits the claimed relevance to 'real-time deployment... in robotics.'

The explanation for why performance is maintained (CEM's robustness to noise, redundancy of ViT features) is largely descriptive/post-hoc and not tightly connected to a predictive theory; the noise-robustness experiment in the appendix uses a strong simplifying assumption (zero-mean Gaussian, uncorrelated with input) that is not rigorously justified.

The method's single notable design novelty, randomized grouped attention, is only ablated on relative L2 prediction error and tied loosely to downstream success improvements; a more rigorous quantitative link (e.g., correlation analysis, statistical test) between prediction error reduction and planning success is missing.

Planning time efficiency gains, while present, are relatively modest at the dropout ratios where performance is maintained (30-50% time reduction at 50% drop), and the comparison is against a somewhat unoptimized Full-Patch baseline rather than other efficient world model architectures, limiting the significance of the efficiency claim.

The paper's writing overstates the contribution ('novel approach', 'thorough experimental analysis') for what is fundamentally an engineering combination of pre-existing ideas (patch dropout, grouped/local attention, DINO-WM), which is a significant but not groundbreaking contribution for a top-tier venue.

strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem: the computational bottleneck of dense patch-token world models during MPC-based planning, which is highly relevant for real-time robotics applications.

The proposed method (random token dropout at inference + randomized grouped attention training) is simple, architecture-agnostic, and easy to integrate into existing transformer-based world models such as DINO-WM.
Extensive experimental evaluation across six diverse environments (navigation, rigid and deformable manipulation) with both success-rate and planning-time metrics.

Thorough set of analyses attempting to explain *why* sparse imagination works: nHSIC mutual-information analysis, attentive probing, an ablation isolating the contribution of grouped attention, and a noise-injection robustness study connecting to CEM's known noise tolerance.

A useful and somewhat counter-intuitive empirical finding: several more sophisticated token-selection/merging methods (LTRP, STAR, Attention-based pruning, agglomerative clustering) do not outperform simple random dropout, and are often computationally more expensive, which is a valuable negative result for the community.
Good reproducibility: detailed appendix with dataset statistics, architecture/hyperparameters, and implementation details for all compared baselines.
weaknesses: Core novelty is incremental: random patch dropout for ViTs is an established idea (e.g., PatchDropout, cited as [29]); the main new pieces are its application to world-model MPC rollouts and the randomized grouped attention training trick, which is a fairly small architectural addition.

Statistical robustness of the main results is unclear: success rates in Table 1 are based on quite small numbers of episodes (20-60), no variance/confidence intervals or multiple seeds are reported, and the numbers are non-monotonic with drop ratio in ways that are hard to interpret (e.g., 50% dropout outperforming the Full baseline in several environments), making it difficult to assess whether reported differences are meaningful or noise.

Primary baselines are limited to Full-Patch and CLS-token variants of the same underlying architecture; there is no comparison against other efficient-planning or model-compression approaches for world models beyond the token-selection ablation, nor against the original DINO-WM numbers/settings for external validation.

Practical guidance is weak: while the paper shows a range of "safe" dropout ratios (~10-50%), the optimal ratio varies substantially by task/environment, and no principled or adaptive method for selecting p is proposed, limiting real-world applicability of the "adaptive" claim made in the abstract.

Explanatory analyses (HSIC, probing, UMAP noise correlation) are largely correlational and somewhat qualitative (e.g., 'no obvious pattern' from visual inspection of UMAP plots) rather than rigorous causal or theoretical support for the core claims.

All experiments are conducted in simulation only; the paper explicitly acknowledges the lack of real-robot validation, which is an important gap given the stated motivation of real-time robotics deployment.

The interaction between training-time grouped attention (binary partition into two groups) and inference-time arbitrary-ratio dropout is not fully justified theoretically, and it's unclear how well this generalizes to arbitrary sparsity patterns/ratios not seen during training.

strengths: The paper conducts an unusually extensive empirical study across 8 simulated environments (Pointmaze, Wall, PushT, Granular, Rope, Block Pushing, LIBERO-10, Meta-World) and 2 real-world robot tasks with an SO-101 arm, providing broad coverage of the claim's applicability.

Careful and fair comparison against a wide range of alternative token-selection strategies (random/LHS, LTRP, Attention-Encoder/STAR/Attention-WM, ATC clustering), consistently showing that simple random dropout is competitive or superior, which is a useful negative result for the field.

The 'blind spot' explanation for why static importance-based pruning underperforms in dynamic planning is a nice mechanistic insight, and it is backed by a quantitative blind-spot occurrence analysis (Table 12) as well as HSIC/attentive-probing information-sufficiency analyses.
Demonstrates real-world deployment value by integrating with a modern VLA (SmolVLA) and showing latency reductions with maintained success rates on physical robot tasks (PickPlace, Drawer).

Substantial ablation studies (architecture generalization across DINO/MoCo-v3/MAE/DINOv3, robustness to synthetic noise, compatibility with gradient-based planners, detailed latency breakdown, LPIPS-based prediction-quality checks, and a preliminary adaptive dropout mechanism) that support robustness of the core claim.
Detailed reproducibility appendix with hyperparameters, dataset descriptions, and implementation details for baselines.
weaknesses: Core technical novelty is limited: the central mechanism (random token dropout at inference, applied to a transformer trained with dropout-like masking) closely follows existing PatchDropout/masking literature already cited by the authors; the main new ingredient (randomized grouped attention training) is a relatively incremental architectural tweak.

Many reported success rates are low and non-monotonic with respect to drop ratio (e.g., Table 1 Pointmaze: 90.0% at 20% drop but 100.0% at 50% drop and 83.3% at 60% drop), suggesting high variance given small evaluation sizes (as few as 20-60 episodes per environment) with no reported confidence intervals or statistical significance testing.
Real-world evaluation is very limited in scale (only 10 trials per task for PickPlace/Drawer), which is insufficient to draw statistically robust conclusions about matching Full-Patch performance.

Performance degrades substantially beyond ~50-60% drop ratio in several environments (e.g., PushT falls from 75% to 20-28% at 90% drop), and while this is expected, the paper's framing sometimes understates how narrow the 'safe' operating range actually is.

Baseline token-selection methods (LTRP, STAR, ATC) were originally designed for single-image classification/segmentation and required nontrivial adaptation to the sequential/goal-conditioned planning setting; it's unclear whether their comparatively weak performance reflects a fundamental limitation or simply suboptimal adaptation/tuning for this new setting.

The 'blind spot' phenomenon and the advantage of unbiased random coverage over static importance-based selection is an intuitively expected outcome once articulated, somewhat limiting the surprise/novelty of this explanatory contribution.
The paper is very dense and relies heavily on the (very long) appendix for many of its central empirical claims and ablations, which may hurt clarity and self-containedness of the main text.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning 8 simulated environments, 2 real-world robot tasks, multiple planning paradigms (MPC-CEM, open-loop CEM, policy-guided/VLA planning, gradient-based MPC), and multiple vision backbones (DINO, MoCo-v3, MAE, DINOv3), showing broad applicability of the core idea.

The identification and characterization of the 'blind spot' problem for static importance-based token selection methods in dynamic planning is a genuinely interesting empirical observation, supported by a reasonably thorough analysis (nHSIC, attentive probing, cluster retention entropy, blind-spot occurrence rate counting).

Detailed latency profiling (Appendix B.8) convincingly shows that the efficiency gains come from the quadratic reduction in self-attention cost, and the comparison to clustering-based alternatives (Appendix B.4) demonstrates a clear practical advantage of simple dropout over more complex merging/clustering methods in terms of wall-clock overhead.
Reasonable reproducibility effort with detailed appendices on datasets, hyperparameters, and baseline implementations.
Real-world demonstration integrating with a modern VLA (SmolVLA) on a physical robot arm is a nice applied contribution showing practical relevance.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is quite thin: it amounts to applying inference-time random patch dropout (a well-known idea, c.f. PatchDropout, which is explicitly cited as prior training-time work) to world-model rollouts, combined with a simple binary randomized-grouping attention mask during training. Neither component is conceptually novel; the main 'contribution' is largely an engineering combination and an empirical observation (random beats fancier selection), which limits the paper's scientific depth for a top-tier venue.

Statistical rigor of the main results is weak: success-rate tables (e.g., Table 1) are based on very small numbers of evaluation episodes (20-60), with no reported variance, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds for the headline planning results. Several entries show dropout ratios outperforming the Full baseline (e.g., 100% at 50% drop in Pointmaze), which is more plausibly noise than a genuine effect, undermining claims of 'maintaining' or even 'improving' performance.

The real-world robot evaluation is extremely small-scale (10 trials each for PickPlace and Drawer), which is far too limited to support confident claims about matching full-patch planning performance or practical deployability.

The explanation for why random sampling outperforms importance-based pruning (the 'blind spot' hypothesis) is plausible but only weakly validated — the supporting experiments (e.g., single Wall environment vision-only ablation, single PushT blind-spot-rate computation) are narrow and environment-specific, yet the paper generalizes this into a strong, repeatedly emphasized headline claim.

Baselines for token-selection comparisons (LTRP, STAR, Attention-Encoder, ATC) are off-the-shelf methods originally designed for static image tasks (classification, reconstruction) and are not adapted/trained for the dynamic planning setting; this risks being a somewhat unfair comparison that inflates the apparent superiority of random sampling rather than demonstrating a fundamental limitation of importance-based selection per se.

The paper lacks comparison against alternative, more established approaches to improving world-model/planning efficiency (e.g., more compact latent world models like Dreamer-style vector representations beyond the weak CLS-token baseline, distillation, smaller backbones, or token merging methods with proper adaptation), making it hard to assess the significance of the proposed approach relative to the broader efficiency literature.

The adaptive dropout mechanism (Appendix B.6) is presented as only a preliminary 'feasibility study' and does not outperform a well-tuned fixed ratio, so it does not meaningfully address the stated limitation that the optimal ratio is task-dependent.

Overall framing oversells a simple empirical finding ('random dropout is a powerful, near-zero overhead strategy') as a general and novel contribution, when the result is arguably an expected consequence of known ViT redundancy work already cited by the authors; the paper would benefit from either deeper theoretical justification or substantially more rigorous, larger-scale evaluation to support such broad claims.

strengths: Very extensive empirical validation spanning 8 simulated environments (Pointmaze, Wall, PushT, Granular, Rope, Block Pushing, LIBERO-10, Meta-World) and 2 real-world robot tasks with SO-101, plus integration with a state-of-the-art VLA (SmolVLA), demonstrating broad applicability of the method.

The 'blind spot' analysis explaining why static importance-based token selection underperforms unbiased random sampling in dynamic planning is a genuinely interesting scientific insight that goes beyond a simple engineering trick, and is well supported by quantitative evidence (blind-spot occurrence rates, cluster retention entropy, HSIC and attentive-probing analyses).

Thorough comparison against a wide range of token-reduction baselines across four families (random sampling, learning-based pruning, attention-based pruning, clustering/merging), showing consistently that complex methods do not outperform simple random dropout, which is a useful negative result for the community.

Solid ablations on architectural generalization (MoCo-v3, MAE, DINOv3 encoders), robustness to noise, different planning paradigms (CEM vs gradient-based MPC), and a detailed latency breakdown confirming the efficiency gains stem from self-attention reduction.

Practical, near-zero-overhead deployment advantage over learned/attention-based selection methods (no extra network or clustering computation needed), demonstrated concretely with real-world latency reductions and successful physical robot deployment.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility information in the appendix (hyperparameters, dataset details, training details for all baselines).
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is modest: random token dropout at test time is a simple idea closely related to prior patch dropout works (e.g., PatchDropout, Liu et al. 2023b), and the randomized grouped attention training strategy, while useful, is an incremental architectural tweak rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Many evaluation settings use small sample sizes (e.g., 20 evals for Granular, 30 for Rope, 50-60 for others; 10 trials for real-world tasks), and the performance trends across drop ratios in Table 1 are non-monotonic and noisy, raising questions about statistical significance of the reported 'no performance loss' claims at specific ratios.

The paper positions efficiency gains as the main selling point, but the actual optimal drop ratio varies substantially by task/environment (as acknowledged in Limitations), undermining the practicality of a single recommended operating point (e.g., 50%) and requiring per-task tuning that is not deeply addressed (the adaptive dropout experiment in App. B.6 is explicitly preliminary).

Missing comparison/discussion of broader efficient world-model literature beyond ViT token-pruning methods (e.g., compressed or hierarchical latent world models, alternative sparsification schemes), which would better contextualize the significance of the contribution relative to non-token-level efficiency approaches.

Real-world validation is limited in scope (only 2 tasks, small number of trials), which, combined with manually selected goal images/states for planning, limits the strength of claims about real-time deployment robustness.

The main text is dense with numeric results and could be better organized to foreground the key scientific narrative (blind spots and information redundancy) rather than reading largely as a benchmark sweep across many tasks and ratios.
